cues.text: A Pope Who Reformed the Church

By the year 595, Gregory I had been Bishop of Rome for five years, having reluctantly accepted the papacy after a distinguished career as a Roman civil administrator, monk, and papal envoy to Constantinople.

He would spend his fourteen years as pope reorganizing the Church's charitable works, reforming its liturgy, and sending missionaries as far as Anglo-Saxon England — a legacy substantial enough that history remembers him simply as Gregory the Great.
It is within this active and demanding pontificate, tradition holds, that one of the earliest surviving Eucharistic accounts of the medieval Church took place.
Laughter in the Communion Line
It was the custom of the age, tradition relates, for the faithful themselves to prepare and bring the bread that would be consecrated at Mass.
One Sunday, Gregory distributed Holy Communion in the ancient basilica built over the tomb of St. Peter.
He noticed one woman in line, among those who had prepared bread that day, laughing openly as she approached.
Troubled, the pope pressed her for an explanation.

She admitted, tradition says, that she could not bring herself to believe that the very bread she had kneaded and baked with her own hands could, through the words of consecration, become the Body of Christ.
An Answer in Flesh and Blood
Rather than simply correct her, Gregory is said to have withheld Communion from her and turned instead to prayer, asking God to resolve what argument alone could not.
When he rose from prayer, tradition holds, the very portion of bread she had prepared had visibly become flesh, marked with blood, in place of its former appearance.
Seeing what her own disbelief had brought about, the woman is said to have fallen to the ground in tears and repentance.
Whatever the precise course of that Sunday Mass, the account handed down insists it was witnessed publicly, by a pope already renowned for holiness in his own lifetime.
Preserved Across the Centuries
The earliest surviving written account connecting this event to Gregory appears in a life of the pope traditionally attributed to Paul the Deacon.
The Lombard monk and historian compiled it toward the end of the eighth century, a gap of roughly two hundred years.
In the careful language of tradition, this places it among early testimony rather than a strictly contemporary record.
Later medieval devotion held that a portion of the relic eventually made its way north to the Benedictine abbey of Andechs in Bavaria.
Local tradition still venerates it there today, though this later chain of custody rests on devotional rather than documentary sources.
It cannot be independently confirmed with the same confidence as the account's origin.
Legacy

Centuries before the more famous accounts of Bolsena or Lanciano would draw pilgrims from across Europe, this quieter Roman episode had already tied the doctrine of the Real Presence to one of the Church's most revered popes.
He was remembered above all for his humility, having styled himself "servant of the servants of God."
Gregory's response was neither anger nor dismissal, but prayer.
The Church has returned to this pattern again and again whenever faith in the Eucharist has wavered.
It trusts that the same Lord who answered a pope's prayer in sixth-century Rome still meets sincere doubt with mercy today.
